title: Build vs Buy inference playbook: vLLM/TGI/TensorRT-LLM comps
body:
Purpose:
This is a pragmatic sales/field playbook for conversations where customers are evaluating building an in-house inference stack (vLLM, TGI, TensorRT-LLM, Triton-based recipes) vs buying Redwood’s hosted / dedicated / private inference offering. The goal is to give AE/SE/PMMs a short, repeatable set of messages, objections, facts, and a lightweight TCO/back-of-envelope so teams can rapidly position Redwood vs a DIY path.

Top-line positioning summary (one-liners):
- For product teams that need predictable latency, operational SLAs, and fast time-to-market, Redwood removes infrastructure risk and scales cost-effectively without the long tail of infra maintenance.
- For infra-heavy orgs intent on owning every layer for raw cost optimization and flexibility, there’s a viable DIY route — but it’s frequently more costly and slower than expected once ops and reliability are included.

Primary buyer personas and motivations:
- Platform / Infra Lead: obsessed with VM/GPU efficiency, curious about kernel-level optimizations; sensitive to open-source control.
- ML Engineer / ML Platform: cares about throughput, fine-tuning latency distributions, and tooling to manage KV cache and batching.
- Product/Engineering PM: wants predictable cost, fast iterations, and minimal ops overhead.
- Security/Compliance (enterprise): needs data residency, KMS, audit logs — willing to pay for private deployments.

Competitor landscape (short snapshot):
- vLLM (community ecosystem): very flexible, excellent KV/cache primitives, great for research and early prototyping; relies on community-maintained kernels and ops patterns. Pros: cheaper entry, full control. Cons: brittle operational assumptions at scale, sparse enterprise support.
- TGI (Text Generation Inference): strong orchestration for multiple model types, good for multi-framework setups and custom transforms. Pros: developer-friendly APIs, plugin ecosystem. Cons: needs infra glue, not tuned for production SLAs out-of-the-box.
- TensorRT-LLM / TRT-based stacks: best raw latency for NVIDIA hardware when models are supported/compatible. Pros: excellent per-token cost on supported models/hardware. Cons: narrow compatibility, engineering effort for quantization and kernel tuning, limited multi-vendor portability.
- Triton-based homebrew: flexible serving with multi-model support; common at companies with mature infra teams. Cons: expensive to maintain, requires deep ops expertise and model-specific optimizations.

Key customer pain narratives to use in pitch:
- "We can build it cheaper" — call out hidden costs: ongoing ops headcount, 24/7 support, debugging latency regressions, model compatibility churn, and integration testing across quantization profiles.
- "We want control" — acknowledge validity; position Redwood Private as an option that preserves control + reduces operational toil (VPC, on-prem, KMS).
- "We don't trust vendors" — emphasize our transparent performance profiles, audit logs, and third-party benchmarks; offer pilot with tech support and playbooks.

Back-of-envelope TCO (3-year, medium-scale inference workload):
- DIY assumptions: 4 engineers (50% FTE on infra/workload support), 2 SREs, misc cloud costs, GPU instances + licensing + time for kernel tuning.
  - Estimated cost: $2.2M - $3.1M (includes people + infra + incident overhead).
- Redwood Hosted + Dedicated mix: predictable per-token + baseline dedicated compute for tail events, managed updates and SLAs, 0.5 FTE from customer for integration/obs.
  - Estimated cost: $1.1M - $1.8M (depending on committed capacity and burst options).
Notes: these are intentionally directional — use for field conversations only and follow up with data team for exact quotes.

Technical decision matrix (short):
- If customer needs sub-10ms p95 on GPU for a specific model on NVIDIA A10X and has deep kernel customization: DIY/TensorRT may win.
- If customer needs multi-model catalog, developer ergonomics, predictable scaling & fallbacks across regions: Redwood is advantaged.
- If regulatory controls + air-gap required: Redwood Private or Dedicated with explicit SLAs.

Operational risk map (what typically trips DIY teams):
- Model drift + silent quality regressions (no systematic evals tied to deployment).
- Queue/backpressure and tail latency bursts under real traffic patterns.
- Patch/tuning churn when upgrading CUDA drivers/TF/PyTorch/quantization stacks.
- Lack of standardized fallback policies across regions and hardware.

Recommended sales plays and messaging snippets:
- For startups & product teams: "Ship features today, optimize later — Redwood lets you iterate without owning the whole stack."
- For infra / platform teams: "Keep control of model artifacts; let us handle serving economics and runtime upgrades — our Dedicated plan gives predictable throughput and tooling for ops."
- For enterprise/security: "We can mirror your compliance posture with Private deployments, KMS integration, and audit-grade telemetry."

Objection handling (practical):
- "We can optimize costs ourselves." -> "Yes, but let’s quantify the ops cost. We offer a 3-6 month pilot where we instrument your workload and show realistic per-token economics vs your projections."
- "We need deterministic latency on specific GPUs." -> "We can benchmark your exact model on our dedicated pool or run a private lab test; where TensorRT is the clear winner we recommend a mixed strategy with Redwood handling fallbacks and routing policies to keep UX stable."

Battlecard quick facts (for SEs):
- Setup time: DIY 6–12 months to stable; Redwood hosted: hours–days; Dedicated: weeks.
- Core tradeoff: control vs operational risk; our sweet spot is teams who want control over models but not over runtime economics and reliability.
- Unique Redwood levers: automatic KV/prefix caching, routing-based fallbacks, per-token cost breakdown in console, rollout policies with automatic fallback.

Packaging recommendations to use in conversations:
- Starter: Hosted API with usage tiers and basic observability (lowest friction).
- Scale: Dedicated pools + monthly commit for predictable throughput; include standard rollout and tracing hooks.
- Regulated: Private deployment (VPC or on-prem) with enterprise SLA and compliance add-on.

Win-loss patterns (observed):
- Win: midmarket SaaS product with strict latency profile but no large infra org — choose Redwood Dedicated for predictable ops and easy rollouts.
- Loss: deep infra-first company (GPU-owning) that values absolute lowest possible per-token cost and has >8 FTEs in infra — often build, but may still ask for hybrid options.

Playbook next steps for field teams (practical checklist):
- For qualifying calls: ask about existing infra headcount, model types, peak qps, p95 latency SLOs, security/regulatory constraints.
- Offer a 2-week pilot: benchmark their top 3 models, instrument cost/latency, and build a migration plan.
- If customer leans build: propose a hybrid migration path and offer Consulting/Professional Services to accelerate early-stage rollout (reduce time-to-1st-success).

Notes-to-self & open questions (work-in-progress):
- Create a short benchmarking kit that AEs can request which runs vLLM/TGI/Trt-LLM comparisons on sample models; link to GH PR above.
- Align pricing team on a 6–12 month pilot credit package for competitive tests (internal Jira: JIRA-GTM-402).
- We should codify a standard one-page ROI sheet for the 3-year TCO comparison — engineering to provide conservative numbers.

References / helpful links:
- GitHub benchmark PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/benchmarks/pull/182
- Internal confluence: confluence:gtm/inference-playbooks
